title: Is this quality approach appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether a way of applying or tailoring the quality practice is fit for purpose, and choose the reason that explains it.
question: Draycott's project manager replaces the standard quality procedure with the company's own aerospace procedures and records the choice in the PID. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?

teach.h: Four tests for any quality decision
teach.body: Test a quality decision four ways. Requirements: is quality driven by backlog items with clear, measurable acceptance criteria? Place: is each thing in the right artifact, with agile behaviours and testing methods in the quality management approach and results in the registers? Done: is the Definition of Done honoured, with no 'almost done'? Fit: do the techniques suit the product, with testing decided early, technical debt under a tolerance and any in-house procedure recorded in the PID?

root.label: A quality decision in the scenario

teach.h: Fit for purpose or poor fit?

rows.label: Partly done story
values: Split: done part done, rest to backlog

rows.label: Supplier testing
values: Documented and assured in the QMA

rows.label: Own procedures
values: Used and recorded as tailoring in the PID
Used with no record of the choice

rows.label: Technical debt
values: Tolerance set; exception if forecast too high

teach.caption: Only the last state is done. A story that is partly finished is split, and the unfinished part returns to the backlog (9.3.2.2).

teach.body: Two questions sit behind every test. Validation asks whether you are building the right thing: does it meet users' real needs? Verification asks whether you are building the thing right: does it meet its specification? A/B testing supports validation by showing users two versions and letting their responses guide the decision. A product can pass verification and still fail validation.

Quality manager Mei Chen insists every change to maintenance follows the aerospace quality system. Project manager Andrea Lucas uses those procedures in place of the standard procedure and records the decision as tailoring in the PID. The quality management approach documents Senticore's fitting checks and the software team's automated tests. The team's Definition of Done includes 'sensor fitted externally, with no change affecting safety certification'. Engineers trial each dashboard view on the shop floor, checking it is the right thing to build.

steps.label: Locate
steps.sub: Which artifact or technique is in play?

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: Choose the one that explains this case

teach.text: Traps: 'partly done stories are split' is true, but splitting moves only a genuinely done part to done; a story counted as finished while defects are open is simply not done. 'The quality register records checks' is true, but it does not show whether a product has been accepted. Test-first thinking is not limited to software, but moving it to other products needs care. An in-house procedure is acceptable when the choice is recorded as tailoring in the PID.

items: Fit for purpose = clear criteria, right artifact, DoD honoured, technique suits the product.
Agile behaviours and testing methods, including suppliers', go in the quality management approach.
No 'almost done': defects mean not done; split genuinely partial stories.
In-house design, development and testing procedures are fine if recorded as tailoring in the PID.
Validation = right thing; verification = thing right; A/B testing lets users decide.

summary: You can now judge whether a quality approach in a scenario is fit for purpose by checking its criteria, its use of artifacts, its Definition of Done and the fit of its techniques. You can also pick the reason that explains the verdict rather than a true statement beside the point.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team is writing a new training course for contact centre advisers. It decides at the start to pilot each module with a few advisers as soon as it is written, accepting that the course cannot be rebuilt as quickly as software. How well does this apply the quality practice, and why?
options: Well, because the testing approach is adapted to the product
Well, because the quality register replaces the DoD
Poorly, because a course is tested once it is all written
Poorly, because module pilots belong in the business case
A.why: PRINCE2 Agile advises deciding early how much can be tested or checked first or as you go, taking care when moving the idea beyond software (9.4.3).

whyNot.1: The quality register records checks and results; it does not replace the Definition of Done.
whyNot.2: Agile prefers test or check first, or at least as you go, rather than testing everything at the end.
whyNot.3: Piloting modules is a quality check, not part of the business justification.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's project manager, Rhys Pengelly, wants the agile behaviours the teams have agreed, such as openly sharing review results, to be documented and properly assured. He has written them into the communication management approach. What should he do instead?
options: Record them in the quality register
Record them in the lessons log
Record them in the commercial management approach
Record them in the quality management approach
A.why: Agile ways of working should be incorporated and documented in the quality management approach, so that agile behaviours are part of it and properly assured (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities, not the behaviours to be assured.
whyNot.1: The lessons log records lessons learned; it does not set out the behaviours the project will assure.
whyNot.2: The commercial management approach covers supplier engagement and contracts, not agile behaviours.

A.q: Callowmere University's quality team wants evidence that each release of the Student Support Hub has been tested with real students. Project manager Jamal Hussain proposes to show it the product register. How well does this apply the quality practice, and why?
options: Well, because it shows each product's acceptance date
Well, because the product register lists every test
Poorly, because evidence belongs in the lessons report
Poorly, because test results sit in the quality register
A.why: The quality register records each quality activity with its method, dates, responsibilities, result and records; the product register shows products and their status (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Acceptance dates show status, not evidence of how and with whom each release was tested.
whyNot.1: The product register lists products and their status, not the tests carried out.
whyNot.2: The lessons report shares lessons for future work; it is not the record of quality activities.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team builds the carers' self-assessment exactly to its written specification. When carers try it, many say it does not ask about the support they actually need, and social workers agree. Which quality concern does this show?
options: Validation: whether the right thing is built
Verification: whether the thing is built right
Refactoring: whether the structure is clean
Technical debt: whether shortcuts remain
B.why: Validation asks whether the right thing is being built for users' needs; the form matches its specification but not the need (9.4.3).

whyNot.1: Verification checks the product against its specification, which this form meets.
whyNot.2: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour; the issue here is the users' needs.
whyNot.3: Technical debt is work owed from poor design; the concern here is that the specification missed the need.

B.q: At Callowmere University's sprint review, the 'track my request' story is partly finished. The status view is built and meets the Definition of Done, but the email notification part has not been started. What should happen to the story?
options: Carry the whole story into the next sprint unchanged
Count half of its story points as done this sprint
Split it: the done part to done, the rest to the backlog
Record it as accepted in the product register
B.why: If a story is partly done before a review, it is split: the done part moves to done and the rest goes back to the backlog for reprioritization (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Carrying it over unchanged hides the done part; the guidance is to split the story.
whyNot.1: There is no 'almost done' or partial credit; work is done or not done.
whyNot.3: The unfinished part is not done, so the whole story cannot be recorded as accepted.

B.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance project is in initiation. Ruth Kenyon, representing the maintenance team, asks where the criteria for the whole project product to be acceptable to her team will be agreed. Where should this happen?
options: In each team planning workshop, in the product backlog
In the release planning workshop, in the release map
In the progress review workshop, on the project dashboard
In project initiation, linked from the project backlog
B.why: The project Definition of Done, the criteria for work to be acceptable to users, is a topic of the project initiation workshop, and the project backlog shows or links to it (Table 13.7, 8.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Team planning refines the team's product backlog for the next iteration; the project-level DoD is agreed in initiation.
whyNot.1: Release planning at stage boundaries updates OKRs and the release map, not the project DoD.
whyNot.2: Progress reviews look at status and demos; they do not set the project DoD.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's store operations team, which uses Kanban, is writing training materials for click and collect. At the start of the stage it agrees to trial each part of the materials in one store as it is written, rather than checking everything once the full pack is finished. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because checking as you go was decided early
Yes, because Kanban teams do not use a Definition of Done
No, because checks should wait until the pack is finished
No, because test-first thinking applies to software products
C.why: A decision should be made early on how much can be tested or checked first or as you go, and the idea can be applied carefully to products other than software (9.4.3).

whyNot.1: A Definition of Done applies to any team's work; this does not explain why trialling as you go is right.
whyNot.2: Agile prefers checking first or as you go rather than leaving quality checks to the end.
whyNot.3: The concept transfers to other products, such as training materials, with care.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team defines a new contact centre script as done when it has been reviewed by the contact centre manager and tested with five tenants. One script has passed the review, but tenant testing found two confusing steps that have not been fixed. Raj Malhotra marks it done because the iteration is ending. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the manager's review has been passed
Yes, because the steps can be fixed next iteration
No, because a script with known problems is not done
No, because tenant testing belongs in the DoR instead
C.why: Something is either done or not done, with no 'almost done'; work with known defects should not be marked done (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: The review is one criterion; the DoD also requires successful tenant testing, which has not been met.
whyNot.1: Unfinished work goes back to the backlog; it is not marked done in the meantime.
whyNot.3: Tenant testing checks whether the work is complete, which is the Definition of Done's job.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's quality management approach sets out the agile ways of working the teams have agreed, including how retrospective actions are followed up. Project assurance then checks that these behaviours are being applied. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
options: Yes, because project assurance writes the quality approach
Yes, because agile behaviours are documented and assured there
No, because behaviours belong in the communication approach
No, because the QMA is limited to test methods and standards
C.why: Agile ways of working should be incorporated and documented in the quality management approach so that agile behaviours are part of it and properly assured (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Project assurance checks adherence; it does not write the quality management approach.
whyNot.2: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication, not assured agile behaviours.
whyNot.3: The QMA does cover techniques and standards, but it also documents agile ways of working and behaviours.

reteach.title: Judging a restaurant kitchen
reteach.question: A head chef runs a busy kitchen. Which of these habits keep quality high, and which should an inspector challenge?

blocks.body: Good: each dish has a clear checklist before it leaves the pass, and a dish with a fault goes back, never out. Tastings are logged with results. The restaurant group's own food safety system is used, and the chef notes that choice in the kitchen manual. Bad: sending a dish out 'nearly right', or keeping tasting results in the staff rota.

rows.label: Pass checklist
values: Dish leaves when it meets it

blocks.text: 'The customer is waiting' is true, but it does not make a faulty dish done. Pick the reason that explains the verdict.

explain.body: The Definition of Done is the team's shared agreement on what complete means. Work either meets it or does not. Defects mean not done; genuinely partial stories are split.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team has built the community directory search. It works, but the easy-read version required by the team's Definition of Done has not been produced. The team proposes to report the story as 'nearly done'. What is the BEST response?
options: Accept it, as the search itself works
Treat it as not done against the DoD
Move the easy-read work into the DoR
Record it as done in the quality register
test.why: An item is done or not done; with a DoD criterion unmet it is not done, and there is no 'nearly done' (9.3.2.2).

whyNot.0: Working search alone does not meet the DoD, so it cannot count as complete.
whyNot.2: The DoR covers readiness to start; moving a completion criterion there would hide unfinished work.
whyNot.3: The quality register records checks and results; it cannot turn incomplete work into done work.

explain.body: Quality evidence goes in the quality register; product status goes in the product register; agile behaviours and testing methods go in the quality management approach.

test.q: Callowmere University's project board asks which products in Release 1 have been approved and accepted so far. Project support prepares the answer from the quality register. How well does this apply the quality practice?
options: Well, as it holds pass and fail results
Well, as it lists every product in the plan
Poorly, as status is in the product register
Poorly, as status is in the lessons log
test.why: The product register lists all products a plan requires and their status, with approval and acceptance dates (Table 9.1).

whyNot.0: Pass and fail results show checks, not whether each product has been approved and accepted.
whyNot.1: Listing products and their status is the product register's job, not the quality register's.
whyNot.3: The lessons log records lessons, not product status.

explain.body: If the business already has design, development and testing procedures, they may be used instead of the standard quality procedure. The choice is documented as a tailoring decision in the PID.

test.q: Draycott Precision Engineering decides to use its aerospace quality system's procedures for designing and approving maintenance changes instead of the standard PRINCE2 Agile quality procedure. Where should this decision be recorded?
options: In the quality register
In the issue register
In the PID, as tailoring
In the lessons log
test.why: Using an alternative procedure should be documented as part of the tailoring decisions in the PID (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: The quality register records quality activities and results, not tailoring decisions.
whyNot.1: The issue register records issues; a planned tailoring choice is not an issue.
whyNot.3: The lessons log records lessons; the tailoring decision itself belongs in the PID.

explain.body: A/B testing shows users two versions of a product or feature and compares their responses to guide the decision. It is a strong check that the right thing is being built.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's digital team cannot agree which of two text message formats tenants will find clearer. It sends version A to half the pilot tenants and version B to the rest, then compares how many reply to confirm their appointment. How well does this apply the quality practice, and why?
options: Well, because the structure is improved by refactoring
Well, because users' responses decide between versions
Poorly, because tenants should not decide the design
Poorly, because both versions must pass the DoR first
test.why: A/B testing compares two versions with users and uses their responses to guide the decision (9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Refactoring changes internal structure without changing behaviour; here two different versions are compared.
whyNot.2: Involving users in quality decisions is central to agile; their response is the evidence.
whyNot.3: The DoR governs when work can start; it is not the reason this test is or is not appropriate.
